sources.license: US Government work; NIST states that information on its sites is public information and may be distributed or copied, with credit requested

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that a process model has the general form of a response variable equal to a mathematical function of predictor variables and parameters plus a random error term, that the predictor variables are also called explanatory variables, independent variables or regressors, that the parameters are unknown quantities estimated during modelling, and that the relationship holds on average across the data and not for each individual observation. All wording, the cohort, and every example in this lesson are original. sources.license: US Government work; NIST states that information on its sites is public information and may be distributed or copied, with credit requested

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that linear least squares obtains parameter estimates by minimising the sum of the squared deviations between the data and the model; that a model is linear when each explanatory variable is multiplied by an unknown parameter, at most one parameter has no corresponding variable, and the terms are summed, so that such a model need not be linear in the explanatory variables themselves; that linear least squares has poor extrapolation properties because model outputs become increasingly extreme as the explanatory variables take extreme values; and that it is highly sensitive to outliers, since one or two unusual points can seriously distort the result and make validation essential. The cohort, every fitted value, and all wording in this lesson are original. NIST copyright guidance at https://www.nist.gov/oism/copyrights states that NIST information is public information that may be distributed or copied and requests appropriate credit.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, section 4.4.4: How can I tell if a model fits my data?
creators: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology, U.S. Department of Commerce
sources.version: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, online edition retrieved 2026-07-25; no publication or revision date is stated on the page

sources.license: US Government work; NIST states that information on its sites is public information and may be distributed or copied, with credit requested

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that residuals are the differences between the observed responses and the corresponding predictions, that residuals behaving randomly suggest the model fits the data well while non-random structure in the residuals indicates it does not, that a high R-squared value does not guarantee that the model fits the data well, and that graphical residual analysis is the primary tool for judging model fit with numerical methods playing a confirmatory role. The residual values, the residual plot, and every worked figure in this lesson are computed from the block's own data and expressed in original wording. NIST copyright guidance at https://www.nist.gov/oism/copyrights states that NIST information is public information that may be distributed or copied and requests appropriate credit.

sources.license: US Government work; NIST states that information on its sites is public information and may be distributed or copied, with credit requested

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that scatter plots of the residuals against the predictor variables in the model and against potential predictors are the main check on the functional part of a model, that residuals exhibiting systematic structure indicate that the form of the function can be improved, and that no single residual plot can completely justify the adoption of a particular model any more than the R-squared statistic can on its own. The three named residual patterns, the constructed nine-point dataset, and all wording in this lesson are original. sources.title: Statistical notes for clinical researchers: covariance and correlation
sources.publisher: Korean Academy of Conservative Dentistry, in Restorative Dentistry & Endodontics
sources.version: Restorative Dentistry & Endodontics 2018;43(1):e4. DOI 10.5395/rde.2018.43.e4. PMCID PMC5816993. PubMed Central full text retrieved 2026-07-25
sources.locator: Sections on the Pearson correlation coefficient: its construction from covariance, its range, the meaning of its sign, and the cautions on interpreting it
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License (CC BY-NC 4.0) as displayed on the article page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that the Pearson correlation coefficient is the standardised form of the covariance, obtained by dividing it by the standard deviations of both variables; that its range is between -1 and +1; that its sign indicates whether the variables move together or in opposite directions; that it reflects only the strength of a linear relationship, so a scatter plot should be inspected before it is calculated; and that identical coefficients can arise from very different underlying relationships, including curved ones and ones distorted by outliers, while a U-shaped relationship can give a coefficient near zero. The licence is Non-Commercial and therefore outside this project's permitted reuse bases, so no wording, figure, table, example, or dataset from the article is reproduced or adapted; the source is used for the underlying facts only and every value in this lesson is computed from the block's own sixty pairs.
